label: lem:framed-parallel
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Put \(\mu=(m_1,\ldots,m_s)\) and \(M=|\mu|=m_1+\cdots+m_s\), and assume that these parts belong to the first component \(K_1\). By the twist eigenvalue and the definition of the signed \(q\)-framing,
\[
\begin{aligned}
Z^\tau_\mu
&=
\sum_{A\vdash M}\chi_A(\mu)
(-a^{-1})^{\tau M}
\mathcal H\!\left(K_1^\tau\star Q_A\cup K_2\cup\cdots\cup K_L;q,a\right)\\
&=
(-a^{-1})^{\tau M}
\mathcal H\!\left(K_1^\tau\star P_\mu\cup K_2\cup\cdots\cup K_L;q,a\right),
\end{aligned}
\]
where
\[
P_\mu=P_{m_1}\cdots P_{m_s}
=\sum_{A\vdash M}\chi_A(\mu)Q_A.
\]
Thus the cycle moment is evaluated by the \(s\) parallel cycle colors in the \(\tau\)-framed tubular neighborhood, multiplied by
\[
(-a^{-1})^{\tau M}.
\]

label: prop:standard-LMOV
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The M\"obius operator in \eqref{eq:PLog} is inverse to the multiple-cover expansion \eqref{eq:standard-reformulated}.  Hence, before dividing the alphabet,
\[
 \operatorname{PLog}Z^{\vec\tau}(x)
 =\sum_{\vec A\ne\vec\varnothing}f^{\vec\tau}_{\vec A}(q,a)s_{\vec A}(x).
\]
By Frobenius' formula and \eqref{eq:divided-alphabet}, componentwise,
\[
 s_A[Y]
 =\sum_{\mu\vdash |A|}
 \frac{\chi_A(\mu)}{\mathfrak z_\mu\{\mu\}}p_\mu(y)
 =\sum_B (M(q)^{-1})_{AB}s_B(y).
\]
Indeed the character table is orthogonal with weight $\mathfrak z_\mu^{-1}$, so the matrices obtained by weighting the $\mu$-column by $\{\mu\}$ and by $\{\mu\}^{-1}$ are inverse.  Therefore the Schur coefficient invariant after the divided-alphabet substitution is $M(q)^{-1}f$, or equivalently $f=M(q)P$.  Taking the tensor product over the link components gives \eqref{eq:fMP}.  This is the standard LMOV change of basis in \cite{LP}.  More explicitly, with $q_{\mathrm{LP}}=q^{-2}$ one has
\[
 q_{\mathrm{LP}}^{-m/2}-q_{\mathrm{LP}}^{m/2}=q^m-q^{-m}=\{m\},
\]
so the matrix \eqref{eq:MAB} is exactly the Liu--Peng matrix \cite{LP} in the present variables (with $t_{\mathrm{LP}}=a^{-2}$).

label: lem:cumulant-contraction
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:cumulant-contraction}
Let $\mathcal L$ be a finite labeled framed link.

\medskip
\noindent
{\rm (i)}
If the labels can be divided into two nonempty groups which are
separated by an embedded $2$-sphere, then
\[
\operatorname{Cum}(\mathcal L)=0.
\]

\medskip
\noindent
{\rm (ii)}
Suppose a local change involves two labels $i$ and $j$, and assume
that for every sublink retaining both labels the corresponding moment
changes by
\[
\Delta M(T)
=
c\,M(T_{i\sim j}),
\qquad
i,j\in T,
\]
where $T_{i\sim j}$ denotes the label set obtained by merging $i$ and
$j$ into a single label.  Assume also that
$
\Delta M(T)=0
$
whenever $T$ omits $i$ or $j$.  Then
\[
\Delta\operatorname{Cum}(\mathcal L)
=
c\,\operatorname{Cum}(\mathcal L_{i\sim j}).
\]
The same conclusion holds termwise for any finite linear combination
of merge operations.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For part~{\rm (i)}, suppose the label set decomposes as
\[
\{1,..,r\}=I\sqcup J,
\qquad
I,J\neq\varnothing,
\]
and the two groups are separated by a $2$-sphere.

Introduce commuting nilpotent variables
$
u_1,\ldots,u_r,
\quad
(u_i^2=0),
$
and form the moment generating polynomial
\[
\mathcal M_{\mathcal L}(u)
=
\sum_{T\subseteq[r]}
M(T)\prod_{i\in T}u_i,
\qquad
M(\varnothing)=1.
\]
The coefficient of
$
u_1\cdots u_r
$
in
$
\log\mathcal M_{\mathcal L}(u)
$
is precisely $\operatorname{Cum}(\mathcal L)$.

Since the two groups are split, every moment factors:
\[
M(T)
=
M(T\cap I)\,M(T\cap J).
\]
Hence we have
$
\mathcal M_{\mathcal L}(u)
=
\mathcal M_{\mathcal L_I}(u_I)
\mathcal M_{\mathcal L_J}(u_J),
$
and therefore
$
\log\mathcal M_{\mathcal L}
=
\log\mathcal M_{\mathcal L_I}
+
\log\mathcal M_{\mathcal L_J}.
$
Neither summand contains a monomial involving variables from both
$I$ and $J$.  Thus the coefficient of
$
u_1\cdots u_r
$
is zero which implies
$
\operatorname{Cum}(\mathcal L)=0.
$

For part~{\rm (ii)}, it is convenient to use the explicit
set-partition formula.  In
\[
\operatorname{Cum}(\mathcal L)
=
\sum_{\pi\in\Pi_r}
(-1)^{|\pi|-1}(|\pi|-1)!
\prod_{B\in\pi}M(B),
\]
a set partition $\pi$ contributes to the change only when $i$ and
$j$ belong to the same block.  Indeed, if they lie in different
blocks, each of those blocks omits one of the two labels, and by
hypothesis its moment does not change.

Suppose $i,j\in B_0\in\pi$.  Since there is only one block containing
both labels,
\[
\Delta
\left(
\prod_{B\in\pi}M(B)
\right)
=
c\,
M((B_0)_{i\sim j})
\prod_{\substack{B\in\pi\\B\neq B_0}}
M(B).
\]
Contracting $i$ and $j$ inside $B_0$ gives a bijection
\[
\left\{
\pi\in\Pi_r:
i,j\text{ lie in the same block}
\right\}
\longleftrightarrow
\Pi_{r-1},
\]
and this bijection preserves the number of blocks.  Hence
\[
\begin{aligned}
\Delta\operatorname{Cum}(\mathcal L)
&=
c
\sum_{\pi'\in\Pi_{r-1}}
(-1)^{|\pi'|-1}(|\pi'|-1)!
\prod_{B\in\pi'}M(B)
\\
&=
c\,\operatorname{Cum}(\mathcal L_{i\sim j}).
\end{aligned}
\]
Linearity gives the final assertion.

label: lem:ordinary-connected
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Ordinary HOMFLY skein recursion gives $\mathcal H(\mathcal{L})\in z^{-h}\mathbb Z[v,a^{\pm1}]$.  For the connected estimate induct on $h$.  A knot has order at least $z^{-1}$.  For $h>1$, switch mixed crossings until one component splits off.  The endpoint cumulant vanishes.  At every crossing change the skein relation and Lemma \ref{lem:cumulant-contraction} give $z$ times an $(h-1)$-component cumulant, hence an element of $z\,z^{h-3}\mathbb Z[v,a^{\pm1}]$.

label: prop:anchor
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Induct on $k+h$.  For $k=0$ use Lemma \ref{lem:ordinary-connected}.  If $k>0$, choose an ordinary component as an anchor and split it from the other labels by crossing changes.  At a passage through $B_{m_i}$, \eqref{eq:relative-annulus-Bm} supplies $\{m_i\}^2$ and merges that colored label into the ordinary anchor.  At an ordinary crossing the usual skein relation supplies $z$. Finally, the vanishing of the split
endpoint proves
\eqref{eq:anchor}.

label: thm:gcd
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
List the $r$ cycle parts of $\vec\lambda$ as $n_1,\ldots,n_r$, retaining their original link-component assignments, and put $D=\gcd(n_1,\ldots,n_r)$.
Using Lemma~\ref{lem:framed-parallel}.  The framing correction contributed by all labeled cycles is the common Laurent monomial
\[
 u_{\vec\lambda,\vec\tau}
 =(-a^{-1})^{\sum_{j=1}^r\tau_{c(j)}n_j},
\]
where $c(j)$ is the original component carrying the $j$th cycle.  Since every labeled cycle occurs exactly once in every set-partition term, this factor is independent of the block decomposition and is therefore irrelevant to divisibility.

Fix $i$.  Expand only the normalized color $B_{n_i}$ by the integral Newton representative
\[
 b_{n_i}=z\sum_{\nu=0}^{n_i-1}\beta_{i,\nu},
\]
where each $\beta_{i,\nu}$ is an integral Hecke word whose annular closure is one ordinary framed component.  By linearity of the cumulant and Proposition~\ref{prop:anchor}, applied with one ordinary label and the remaining $r-1$ normalized cycle labels,
\[
 \operatorname{Cum}\!\left(\operatorname{cl}(\beta_{i,\nu});B_{n_j},\ j\ne i\right)
 \in\left(\prod_{j\ne i}\{n_j\}^2\right)z^{-1}\mathbb Z[v,a^{\pm1}].
\]
The explicit factor $z$ in $b_{n_i}$ cancels the knot pole $z^{-1}$.  Hence, for every $i$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:gcd-step-one}
 \check F^{\vec\tau}_{\vec\lambda}
 \in\left(\prod_{j\ne i}\{n_j\}^2\right)\mathbb Z[v,a^{\pm1}].
\end{equation}

Now, set $A_j(v)=\{n_j\}^2\in\mathbb Z[v]$ and $T(v)=\prod_jA_j(v)=\{\vec\lambda\}^2$.  The divisors in \eqref{eq:gcd-step-one} are $G_i=T/A_i$.  Since every $G_i$ is monic, divisibility by all $G_i$ implies divisibility by their monic least common multiple, denoted by $\operatorname{lcm}_i(G_i)$.  For an irreducible polynomial $\phi(v)\in\mathbb Q[v]$, write $a_j=\operatorname{ord}_\phi A_j$.  Then
\[
 \operatorname{ord}_\phi\operatorname{lcm}_i(G_i)
 =\max_i\left(\sum_j a_j-a_i\right)
 =\sum_j a_j-\min_i a_i.
\]
Thus, we obtain
\[
 \operatorname{lcm}_i(G_i)
 =\frac{\prod_jA_j}{\gcd(A_1,\ldots,A_r)}.
\]
Now $\{m\}=q^{-m}(q^{2m}-1)$ and
$\gcd(q^{2m}-1,q^{2n}-1)=q^{2\gcd(m,n)}-1$.  Up to Laurent monomial units this gives
$\gcd(\{m\},\{n\})=\{\gcd(m,n)\}$.  Since the squares $\{m\}^2$ are monic polynomials in $v$, it follows that
\[
 \gcd\bigl(\{n_1\}^2,\ldots,\{n_r\}^2\bigr)=\{D\}^2.
\]
Consequently, we have
\[
 \operatorname{lcm}_{1\le i\le r}\prod_{j\ne i}\{n_j\}^2
 =\frac{\{\vec\lambda\}^2}{\{D\}^2}.
\]
Therefore, it proves the first assertion in \eqref{eq:gcd}.

By definition,
\(
 H^{\vec\tau}_{\vec\lambda}
 =\frac{\{D\}^2\check F^{\vec\tau}_{\vec\lambda}}{\{\vec\lambda\}^2},
\)
so the preceding divisibility immediately gives
$H^{\vec\tau}_{\vec\lambda}\in\mathbb Z[v,a^{\pm1}]$.

name: Local crossing identities

label: lem:exterior-transport
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:exterior-transport}
Remove a parallel-oriented crossing box from a framed link and replace each exterior arc
by $n$ parallel strands.  If the exterior is packet-preserving, it commutes with the
packet algebra $A$.  If it exchanges the packets, it intertwines the two $\mathsf{H}_n$-actions.
These identities remain valid after adding normalized spectator colors supported away
from the two packet ribbons.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Move an internal Hecke coupon along the product tubular neighborhood of the corresponding
exterior ribbon.  The ribbon framing identifies the transverse disks, so this motion is a
framed isotopy.  A packet-preserving exterior returns the coupon to the same packet; a
packet-exchanging exterior returns it to the opposite packet.

label: lem:regular-closure
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:regular-closure}
Assume $\operatorname{ord}(\alpha^2)=n>1$.  Closure of a finite ordinary framed local tangle, possibly
with spectator colors $B_m$, lies in $\mathcal O_\alpha[a^{\pm1}]$.  More generally, an
outside factor $(q-\alpha)^s$ cannot be lowered by closure.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Expand every spectator $B_m$ by the integral Newton representative.  Ordinary HOMFLY--PT
skein reduction then introduces only powers of $z^{-1}$.  Since
$z(\alpha)=\alpha-\alpha^{-1}\ne0$ for $n>1$, these denominators are units in
$\mathcal O_\alpha$.

label: lem:root-framing
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Framing congruence for an $n$-cycle

label: eq:hook-frame
title: Proof
body_md:
This lemma can be regarded as a generalization of the prime-cycle framing congruence in \cite{CLPZ}, but the proof is the same.  The case $\tau=0$ is immediate.  For $\tau\ne0$, character inversion and the
standard hook-character identity give
\begin{equation}\label{eq:hook-frame}
 \check Z_n(K;\tau)
 =a^{n\tau}\frac{\{n\}}{\{n\tau\}}
 \sum_{\mu\vdash n}\frac{\check Z^0_\mu(K)}{\mathfrak z_\mu}
 \prod_{i=1}^{\ell(\mu)}\frac{\{n\tau\mu_i\}}{\{\mu_i\}}.
\end{equation}
If $\mu\ne(n)$, then $\ell(\mu)\ge2$ and every part satisfies $0<\mu_i<n$.
Hence $\{\mu_i\}(\alpha)\ne0$, while $\{n\tau\mu_i\}(\alpha)=0$, so the
corresponding term has order at least two at $q=\alpha$.

For $\mu=(n)$ the coefficient is
\[
 R_{n,\tau}(q)=\frac1n\frac{\{n^2\tau\}}{\{n\tau\}}.
\]
Putting $x=q^{n\tau}$ gives
\[
 R_{n,\tau}(q)=\frac1n\frac{x^n-x^{-n}}{x-x^{-1}}.
\]
At $q=\alpha$, $x=\alpha^{n\tau}=\pm1$, and
$R_{n,\tau}(\alpha)=\varepsilon_n^\tau$.  The Laurent polynomial
$(x^n-x^{-n})/(x-x^{-1})$ is invariant under $x\mapsto x^{-1}$; hence its first
derivative vanishes at the fixed points $x=\pm1$.  Therefore
$R_{n,\tau}(q)=\varepsilon_n^\tau+O((q-\alpha)^2)$, proving the lemma.

label: lem:smoothing-framing
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Framing under oriented smoothing

title: Proof
body_md:
For blackboard framings the formulas follow by comparing self-writhes.  In the mixed case,
after smoothing, every remaining crossing between $K_i$ and $K_j$ becomes a self-crossing
of $K_{ij}$; their signed sum is
$2\operatorname{lk}(K_i,K_j)-\sigma(c)$.  In the self-crossing case, after smoothing,
the crossings between $K'$ and $K''$ have signed sum $2\operatorname{lk}(K',K'')$,
and restoring the removed crossing contributes $\sigma(c)$.  For arbitrary ribbon
framings, the additional full twists add under merging and split additively under
separation.  Reduction modulo two gives the parity statements.

label: prop:uniform-knot
title: Proposition
head: environment
name: Knot congruence

label: eq:knot-upper-recurrence
title: Proof
body_md:
Let $D_+,D_-,D_0$ be a self-crossing triple, with $D_0=K'\cup K''$ carrying the
inherited framings.  The self-crossing identity \eqref{eq:self-main}, together with
Lemmas~\ref{lem:exterior-transport} and \ref{lem:regular-closure}, gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:knot-upper-recurrence}
 \check Z_n(D_+)-\check Z_n(D_-)
 \equiv\varepsilon_n\check Z_{(n,n)}(D_0)
 \pmod{(q-\alpha)^2}.
\end{equation}
By the moment--cumulant formula and Theorem~\ref{thm:gcd},
\begin{equation}\label{eq:knot-upper-factorization}
 \check Z_{(n,n)}(D_0)
 \equiv\check Z_n(K';\tau')\check Z_n(K'';\tau'')
 \pmod{(q-\alpha)^2}.
\end{equation}
For the fundamental cycle, the HOMFLY--PT skein relation gives the exact identity
\[
 \check Z_1(D_+)-\check Z_1(D_-)=\check Z_{(1,1)}(D_0).
\]
Again Theorem~\ref{thm:gcd} gives
$\check Z_{(1,1)}(D_0)-\check Z_1(K';\tau')\check Z_1(K'';\tau'')\in z^2\mathbb Z[v,a^{\pm1}]$.
Applying $\Psi_n$ and using $\Psi_n(z^2)=\{n\}^2$ yields
\begin{equation}\label{eq:knot-lower-factorization}
 \Psi_n\check Z_{(1,1)}(D_0)
 \equiv
 \Psi_n\check Z_1(K';\tau')\,\Psi_n\check Z_1(K'';\tau'')
 \pmod{(q-\alpha)^2}.
\end{equation}
If the induction hypothesis is applied to $K'$ and $K''$, the leading term in
\eqref{eq:knot-upper-recurrence} acquires the sign
$\varepsilon_n^{1+\tau'+\tau''}$.  By
\eqref{eq:self-smoothing-parity}, this equals $\varepsilon_n^{\tau(D)}$.  Thus both sides of
\eqref{eq:uniform-knot} satisfy the same crossing-change recursion.  Switching crossings
to a descending diagram reduces to a framed unknot, where the claim follows from
Lemma~\ref{lem:root-framing} and
$\check Z_n(U;0)=a^n-a^{-n}=\Psi_n\check Z_1(U;0)$.

label: thm:equal-cycle
title: Theorem
head: environment
name: Equal-cycle congruence

label: eq:equal-cycle-recurrence
title: Proof
body_md:
For $r=1$ this is Proposition~\ref{prop:uniform-knot}.  Suppose $r>1$ and choose a mixed
crossing.  The mixed identity \eqref{eq:mixed-main} has leading term
$\varepsilon_n n\{n\}^2$ times the contracted label and remainder divisible by $\{n\}^4$.
Inside the $r$-label cumulant, the remaining $r-2$ normalized cycle labels contribute
$\{n\}^{2(r-2)}$ by Proposition~\ref{prop:anchor}; hence the total unnormalized error is
divisible by $\{n\}^{2r}$.  Dividing by the connected normalization
$\{n\}^{2r-2}$ leaves a second-order error and gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:equal-cycle-recurrence}
 H^{\mathrm{ord}}_{(n^r)}(\mathcal L_+)-H^{\mathrm{ord}}_{(n^r)}(\mathcal L_-)
 \equiv\varepsilon_n n\,H^{\mathrm{ord}}_{(n^{r-1})}(\mathcal L_0)
 \pmod{(q-\alpha)^2}.
\end{equation}
For the fundamental cycle, contraction of connected cumulants gives exactly
\[
 H^{\mathrm{ord}}_{(1^r)}(\mathcal L_+)-H^{\mathrm{ord}}_{(1^r)}(\mathcal L_-)
 =H^{\mathrm{ord}}_{(1^{r-1})}(\mathcal L_0).
\]
Apply the induction hypothesis to $\mathcal L_0$.  By
\eqref{eq:mixed-smoothing-parity},
$\tau(\mathcal L_0)\equiv\tau(\mathcal L)+1\pmod2$, so the extra local factor $\varepsilon_n$ in
\eqref{eq:equal-cycle-recurrence} changes $\varepsilon_n^{\tau(\mathcal L_0)}$ into
$\varepsilon_n^{\tau(\mathcal L)}$.  Hence the difference between the two sides of
\eqref{eq:equal-cycle} is invariant modulo $(q-\alpha)^2$ under mixed crossing changes.
Switch mixed crossings until the labeled link splits into two nonempty groups; both
connected cumulants then vanish by Lemma~\ref{lem:cumulant-contraction}.  The result follows.

label: lem:cable-cycle
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Frobenius' formula and the plethystic identity $p_m(x^D)=p_{mD}(x)$ give
\[
 \sum_{A\vdash m}\chi_A((m))c^B_{A;D}=\chi_B((mD)).
\]
Substituting \eqref{eq:cable-Schur} into the definition of $\check Z_m(J;kD)$
cancels the factors $q^{kD\kappa_A}$, while the $a$-factor simplifies as
$a^{mkD}a^{-mk(D-1)}=a^{mk}$.  The preceding character identity then yields
\eqref{eq:cable-cycle}.

label: lem:finite-slope
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Expand each cycle moment by the finite character sum and the connected coefficient by the
finite set-partition formula.  Every label contributes the common factor $a^{mk_i}$, and
all remaining slope dependence is through $q^{k_i\kappa_{A_i}/D_i}$.  A nonzero
$(mD_i)$-cycle character forces $A_i=(mD_i-b_i,1^{b_i})$, so
\[
 \frac{\kappa_{A_i}}{D_i}=m(mD_i-1-2b_i)\in\mathbb Z.
\]
head: environment

label: lem:hook-root-phase
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Use $\kappa_A=nD(nD-1-2b)$ and $\kappa_B=D(D-1-2c)$.  Since $\omega^2=1$, the hook
labels disappear.  Finally $\omega^{n-1}=\varepsilon_n$: this is immediate if $n$ is odd, while
for even $n$ exact squared order gives $\omega=-1$.

label: lem:interpolation
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:interpolation}
Let $F$ be a field of characteristic zero and suppose
\[
 f(s;k)=\sum_{\nu=1}^MR_\nu(s)(1+s)^{\Lambda_\nu(k)},\qquad k\in\mathbb Z^r,
\]
where the Laurent series $R_\nu(s)\in F((s))$ have a common finite lower bound and the
$\Lambda_\nu$ are integer-valued affine linear forms.  If $\operatorname{ord}_s f(s;k)\ge b$
on a Cartesian product of infinite subsets of $\mathbb Z$, then the same inequality holds for all
$k\in\mathbb Z^r$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For every degree $d<b$, the coefficient $[s^d]f(s;k)$ is a polynomial in the $k_i$ because
$[s^m](1+s)^{\Lambda(k)}=\binom{\Lambda(k)}m$.  A polynomial over a characteristic-zero
field that vanishes on a product of infinite subsets is identically zero.
head: environment

label: thm:universal-slope
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
First assume $k_i\ne0$ and $(k_i,D_i)=1$.  Apply
\eqref{eq:connected-cable-factor} with $m=n$ and $m=1$.  By
\eqref{eq:cable-prefactor-Adams}, both sides have the same cable prefactor after applying
$\Psi_n$.  The cabled components have integer framings $k_iD_i$, so
Theorem~\ref{thm:equal-cycle} gives \eqref{eq:universal-slope} on the product of the
coprime slope grids.

Put $q=\alpha(1+s)$.  By Lemma~\ref{lem:finite-slope}, after factoring out the common
$a$-monomial, every upper summand has root phase
$\rho(k)=\omega^{\sum_i k_i(nD_i-1)}$.  Lemma~\ref{lem:hook-root-phase} shows that the
lower root phase, after multiplication by $\varepsilon_n^{\sum_i k_iD_i}$, is the same
$\rho(k)$.  Dividing by these nonzero common factors leaves a finite sum of the form in
Lemma~\ref{lem:interpolation}.  Since the coprime set
$\{k\in\mathbb Z\setminus\{0\}:(k,D_i)=1\}$ is infinite for every $i$, interpolation extends the
order-two identity to all integer slopes.
head: environment

label: eq:ordinary-final-comparison
title: Proof
body_md:
List all cycle parts of $\vec\nu$ as $D_1,\ldots,D_r$, retaining the original link-component
assignment, and let $\tau_i$ be the framing of the component carrying $D_i$.  In the ordinary framed parallel realization of Lemma~\ref{lem:framed-parallel}, reset the underlying parallel companions to zero individual framing and encode each original integer framing through the algebraic slope parameter.  Thus Theorem~\ref{thm:universal-slope} applies with
\[
 k_i=D_i\tau_i.
\]
Put $S=\sum_i\tau_iD_i$.  Since $D_i^2\equiv D_i\pmod2$, the framing phase in
\eqref{eq:universal-slope} is $\varepsilon_n^S$, and hence
\begin{equation}\label{eq:ordinary-final-comparison}
 H^{\mathrm{ord}}_{n\vec\nu}
 \equiv n^{r-1}\varepsilon_n^S\Psi_nH^{\mathrm{ord}}_{\vec\nu}
 \pmod{(q-\alpha)^2}.
\end{equation}
Lemma~\ref{lem:framed-parallel} gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:signed-ordinary-relation}
 H^{\vec\tau}_{\vec\nu}=(-a^{-1})^S H^{\mathrm{ord}}_{\vec\nu},
 \qquad
 H^{\vec\tau}_{n\vec\nu}=(-a^{-1})^{nS}H^{\mathrm{ord}}_{n\vec\nu}.
\end{equation}
Finally,
\[
 (-a^{-1})^{nS}\varepsilon_n^S
 =\Psi_n\bigl((-a^{-1})^S\bigr).
\]
Multiplying \eqref{eq:ordinary-final-comparison} by $(-a^{-1})^{nS}$ and using
\eqref{eq:signed-ordinary-relation} proves
\[
 H^{\vec\tau}_{n\vec\nu}
 \equiv n^{r-1}\Psi_nH^{\vec\tau}_{\vec\nu}
 \pmod{(q-\alpha)^2},
\]
which is Theorem~\ref{thm:framed-congruence}.

head: environment
name: Rational polynomiality

title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $
\operatorname{ord}(\alpha^2)=e
$
and
$
(\ell,e)=1,
$
we have
\[
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{ord}
\left(
(\alpha^{d\ell})^2
\right)
&=
\operatorname{ord}
\left(
(\alpha^2)^{d\ell}
\right)
\\
&=
\frac{e}{\gcd(e,d\ell)}
\\
&=
\frac{e}{d}.
\end{aligned}
\]


For the case
$
\frac{e}{d}>1, 
$
we set $
m:=\frac{e}{d}$
and
$
\vec\nu
:=
\frac{\vec\lambda}{e\ell}.
$
This is well defined since
$
e\mid D$, $\ell\mid D$ and $
(e,\ell)=1
$
imply that
$
e\ell\mid D.
$
Moreover, we have
$
m\vec\nu
=
\frac{e}{d}
\frac{\vec\lambda}{e\ell}
=
\frac{\vec\lambda}{d\ell}.
$

Applying Theorem~\ref{thm:framed-congruence} with variables $(t,b)$, root
$
\beta=\alpha^{d\ell},
$
cycle tuple $\vec\nu$, and scaling factor $m=e/d$, using
\[
\operatorname{ord}(\beta^2)=m,
\]
we obtain
\[
H_{\vec\lambda/(d\ell)}^{\vec\tau}(t,b)
-
\left(\frac{e}{d}\right)^{r-1}
H_{\vec\lambda/(e\ell)}^{\vec\tau}
\left(
t^{e/d},b^{e/d}
\right)
\in
(t-\beta)^2
\mathcal O_\beta[b^{\pm1}].
\]

Now substitute
$
t=q^{d\ell},\qquad b=a^{d\ell}.
$
Then
$
t-\beta
=
q^{d\ell}-\alpha^{d\ell}
=
d\ell\,\alpha^{d\ell-1}(q-\alpha)
+
O((q-\alpha)^2).
$
Since the coefficient
$
d\ell\,\alpha^{d\ell-1}
$
is nonzero. Therefore,
$
(t-\beta)^2
$
is a unit multiple of
$
(q-\alpha)^2
$
in the local ring at $q=\alpha$. Hence, the substituted identity is exactly
\[
\Psi_{d\ell}
H_{\vec\lambda/(d\ell)}^{\vec\tau}
\equiv
\left(\frac{e}{d}\right)^{r-1}
\Psi_{e\ell}
H_{\vec\lambda/(e\ell)}^{\vec\tau}
\pmod{(q-\alpha)^2}.
\]

For the case $e/d=1$, both sides are identical, so the same formula holds
tautologically.

head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Put $A=\mathbb Z[q^{\pm1},a^{\pm1}]$ and let $S$ be the multiplicative set generated by the invariant elements $\{m\}^2$.  Then $R_0=S^{-1}A$.  Invariance under $q\mapsto -q$ first gives $\mathbb Z[q^{\pm2},a^{\pm1}]$, and invariance there under $q\mapsto q^{-1}$ gives
\[
 A^G=\mathbb Z[q^2+q^{-2},a^{\pm1}]=\mathbb Z[v,a^{\pm1}],
\]
since $q^2+q^{-2}=v+2$.  Because every element of $S$ is fixed by $G$, an invariant fraction $f/s$ with $s\in S$ has invariant numerator: $g(f)/s=f/s$ implies $g(f)=f$ in the domain $A$.  Hence
\[
 (S^{-1}A)^G=S^{-1}(A^G).
\]
Finally $\{m\}^2=vU_m(v)$, which gives \eqref{eq:invariant-localization}.

label: lem:frobenius-lift
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:frobenius-lift}
Fix a prime $p$ and put $R_{0,(p)}=R_0\otimes_\mathbb Z\mathbb Z_{(p)}$.
Let $\Lambda$ be the integral symmetric-function ring, and let
$(\Lambda^{\otimes L})_d$ denote its part of total degree $d$.
Use the graded completion
\[
 A_p=\prod_{d\ge0}
          \bigl(R_{0,(p)}\otimes_\mathbb Z(\Lambda^{\otimes L})_d\bigr).
\]
Then $A_p$ is torsion free and complete for the filtration by total
degree. The Adams operation
\[
 \Psi_p(q)=q^p,\qquad
 \Psi_p(a)=a^p,\qquad
 \Psi_p\bigl(p_m(x^c)\bigr)=p_{pm}(x^c)
\]
extends continuously to $A_p$ and satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{eq:frobenius-lift}
 \Psi_p(F)\equiv F^p\pmod{pA_p}\qquad(F\in A_p).
\end{equation}
The same statement holds after the divided-alphabet substitution
$x\mapsto Y$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Each homogeneous part of $\Lambda^{\otimes L}$ is a finite free
abelian group, and $R_{0,(p)}$ is torsion free. The displayed product
is therefore torsion free and complete.

It is enough to check the Frobenius congruence on integral algebra
generators before passing to the graded completion.
It is immediate for $q^{\pm1}$ and $a^{\pm1}$. Since
\[
 \Psi_p(\{m\})=\{mp\}\equiv\{m\}^p\pmod p
\]
and every $\{m\}$ is a unit in $R_0$, inversion gives
\[
 \Psi_p(\{m\}^{-1})\equiv\{m\}^{-p}\pmod p.
\]
In the integral symmetric-function ring, the freshman's-dream
identity in the underlying variables gives
\[
 p_{pm}(x^c)\equiv p_m(x^c)^p\pmod p.
\]
To check integral generators, apply the same identity to the
complete symmetric functions $h_j$, which generate $\Lambda$
over $\mathbb Z$:
\[
 \Psi_p(h_j(x^c))
   =h_j\bigl((x_1^c)^p,(x_2^c)^p,\ldots\bigr)
       \equiv h_j(x^c)^p\pmod p.
\]
These identities may first be checked in finitely many variables
and then passed to the symmetric-function ring.
Multiplicativity proves the congruence on
$R_{0,(p)}\otimes\Lambda^{\otimes L}$. Since Adams multiplies
degree by $p$, continuity gives \eqref{eq:frobenius-lift} on $A_p$.

 Finally, each Schur coefficient after $x\mapsto Y$ has only quantum-integer denominators, hence belongs to $R_0$; therefore the substitution defines a continuous endomorphism into the same completed ring.

label: lem:dwork
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:dwork}
Fix a prime $p$. Let $B$ be a commutative torsion-free $\mathbb Z_{(p)}$-algebra, and
let $\varphi_p:B\to B$ be an endomorphism satisfying
$\varphi_p(b)\equiv b^p\pmod{pB}$ for every $b\in B$.
Put $A=B[[u_1,\ldots,u_L]]$ and $I=(u_1,\ldots,u_L)$.
Extend $\varphi_p$ continuously to $A$ by
\[
 \psi_p\left(\sum_{\mathbf d}b_{\mathbf d}\mathbf u^{\mathbf d}\right)
       =\sum_{\mathbf d}\varphi_p(b_{\mathbf d})
                                      \mathbf u^{p\mathbf d}.
\]
For $Z\in1+I$, put
\[
 D_p(Z)=\log Z-\frac1p\psi_p(\log Z).
\]
Then $D_p(Z)\in A$. If $\{\varphi_k\}_{k\ge1}$ is a compatible
system of Adams operations on $B$, extended to $\psi_k$ by
$u_c\mapsto u_c^k$, then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:dwork-pairing}
 \sum_{k\ge1}\frac{\mu(k)}k\psi_k(\log Z)
  =\sum_{\substack{k\ge1\\(k,p)=1}}\frac{\mu(k)}k
                                      \psi_k\bigl(D_p(Z)\bigr).
\end{equation}
The sums are interpreted coefficientwise in total $\mathbf u$-degree.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The Frobenius congruence gives $\psi_p(Z)\equiv Z^p\pmod{pA}$.
Both terms are units with constant term one. Consequently, there
is $K\in I$ with
\[
 \frac{Z^p}{\psi_p(Z)}=1+pK.
\]
Here each positive-degree coefficient of the quotient minus one
is divisible by $p$, and its constant coefficient is zero; this
gives $K\in I$ coefficientwise.
Using continuity and $\psi_p(\log Z)=\log\psi_p(Z)$,
\[
 D_p(Z)=\frac1p\log(1+pK)
       =\sum_{j\ge1}(-1)^{j-1}\frac{p^{j-1}}jK^j.
\]
Since $\operatorname{ord}_p(j)\le j-1$, every coefficient belongs to
$\mathbb Z_{(p)}$. The series converges $I$-adically because $K\in I$.
Thus $D_p(Z)\in A$.

For \eqref{eq:dwork-pairing}, terms with $p^2\mid k$ vanish
because $\mu(k)=0$. Every nonzero M\"obius term whose index is
divisible by $p$ is therefore paired uniquely with the term of
index $k$, where $(k,p)=1$. Since $\mu(pk)=-\mu(k)$ and
$\psi_{pk}=\psi_k\psi_p$,
\begin{align*}
 &\frac{\mu(k)}k\psi_k(\log Z)
       +\frac{\mu(pk)}{pk}\psi_{pk}(\log Z)\\
 &\qquad=
 \frac{\mu(k)}k\psi_k
             \left(\log Z-\frac1p\psi_p(\log Z)\right).
\end{align*}
Summing over $(k,p)=1$ gives the identity. This rearrangement is
legitimate: $\psi_k$ multiplies positive total degree by $k$, so
only finitely many terms contribute to a fixed multidegree.

label: lem:primitive-symmetry
title: Lemma
head: environment

label: eq:colored-q-symmetry
title: Proof
body_md:
The standard HOMFLY--PT skein involutions (see, e.g., \cite{LP}), componentwise in the colors, give
\begin{equation}\label{eq:colored-q-symmetry}
 W_{\vec A}^{\vec\tau}(-q,a)
 =(-1)^{|\vec A|}W_{\vec A}^{\vec\tau}(q,a),
 \qquad
 W_{\vec A}^{\vec\tau}(q^{-1},a)
 =(-1)^{|\vec A|}W_{\vec A^t}^{\vec\tau}(q,a).
\end{equation}
The signed $q$-framing factors preserve these formulas because every $\kappa_A$ is even and $\kappa_{A^t}=-\kappa_A$.  On the divided alphabet,
\[
 \{m\}_{-q}=(-1)^m\{m\}_q,
 \qquad
 \{m\}_{q^{-1}}=-\{m\}_q.
\]
Hence 
$p_m(Y_{-q})
=
(-1)^m p_m(Y_q), \ p_m(Y_{q^{-1}})
=
-p_m(Y_q).$
Consequently, we have
\begin{equation}\label{eq:schur-q-symmetry}
s_{\vec A}[Y_{-q}]
=
(-1)^{|\vec A|}s_{\vec A}[Y_q], \ s_{\vec A}[Y_{q^{-1}}]
=
(-1)^{|\vec A|}
s_{\vec A^t}[Y_q].
\end{equation}
Then Lemma \ref{lem:primitive-symmetry} follows from \eqref{eq:colored-q-symmetry} and \eqref{eq:schur-q-symmetry}.

label: prop:localization
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The only possible scalar denominators in the framing-independent
colored invariants $W_{\vec A}$ are quantum integers. One may
compute $W_{\vec A}$ in the preferred zero-framing realization,
where this follows from the projector construction above.
The signed framing multiplier is $(-1)^Eq^K$, with
\[
 E=\sum_b\tau_b|A^b|,\qquad K=\sum_b\tau_b\kappa_{A^b}.
\]
It is a Laurent-monomial unit, so the same localization contains
the framed invariants. It remains to show that the logarithm and
M\"obius combination defining the primitive coefficients leave
no integer denominators in the Schur basis.

Introduce independent degree variables $u_c$ for the link
components. The divided alphabet has the plethystic expression
\[
 Y=\frac{q^{-1}y}{1-q^{-2}}.
\]
The integral Kronecker rule and principal specialization of Schur
functions \cite{Macdonald} show that the Schur coefficients of
$s_A[Y]$ lie in $R_0$. Their hook denominators are products of
$1-q^{-2h}=q^{-h}\{h\}$, as in the proof of
Lemma~\ref{lem:frobenius-lift}.
Thus the degree-recorded partition function is
\[
 Z^{\vec\tau}[u_1Y^1,\ldots,u_LY^L]
   =\sum_{\vec A}W_{\vec A}^{\vec\tau}
                  \prod_c s_{A^c}[Y^c]u_c^{|A^c|}
 \in1+(\mathbf u)
     (R_0\otimes_\mathbb Z\Lambda^{\otimes L})[[\mathbf u]].
\]
Each coefficient of fixed $\mathbf u$-multidegree is a finite
symmetric-function sum. Its degree is recorded by $\mathbf u$;
the series represents the same coefficient data as the graded
completion in Lemma~\ref{lem:frobenius-lift}.

Fix a prime $p$, and put
$B_p=R_{0,(p)}\otimes_\mathbb Z\Lambda^{\otimes L}$.
Work in $B_p[[\mathbf u]]$ with $I=(\mathbf u)$.
The divided partition function lies in $1+I$.
Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:dwork} with $B=B_p$ and the coefficient
Adams operation $\varphi_p=\Psi_p$, extended by
$\psi_p(u_c)=u_c^p$. Lemma~\ref{lem:frobenius-lift} supplies the
Frobenius lift on coefficient variables, inverse quantum integers,
and symmetric-function variables.
Equation \eqref{eq:dwork-pairing} expresses the primitive
logarithm as a sum of $p$-integral Dwork differences indexed by
$(k,p)=1$. In any fixed multidegree, only finitely many terms
contribute, so passage to the corresponding Schur coefficient is
legitimate. Every fixed Schur coefficient is therefore $p$-integral.
Since the divided-alphabet substitution commutes with Adams, these
are the coefficients $P_{\vec A}^{\vec\tau}$ of
\eqref{eq:PLog}, with their degrees recorded by $\mathbf u$.

This holds for every prime. For completeness, the passage to
$\mathbb Z$ may be made coefficientwise. For a fixed coefficient $f$,
choose a nonzero integer $b$ with $bf\in R_0$; only finitely
many rational scalar denominators occur in a fixed multidegree.
For each prime $p\mid b$, the membership $f\in R_{0,(p)}$ supplies
an integer $a_p$ coprime to $p$ with $a_pf\in R_0$.
The integers $b$ and these finitely many $a_p$ have greatest common
divisor one. B\'ezout's identity therefore gives $f\in R_0$.

Every fixed primitive Schur coefficient thus belongs to $R_0$.
Lemma~\ref{lem:primitive-symmetry} shows that it is fixed by both
$q\mapsto-q$ and $q\mapsto q^{-1}$.
Lemma~\ref{lem:invariant-localization} consequently places it in
\[
 R_0^G=\mathbb Z[v,a^{\pm1},\{m\}^{-2}:m\ge1],
\]
which is \eqref{eq:arith-localization}.

title: Proof
body_md:
Proposition~\ref{prop:rational-polynomiality} gives
\[
 vP^{\vec\tau}_{\vec A}\in\mathbb Q[v,a^{\pm1}].
\]
By Proposition~\ref{prop:localization}, write
\[
 P^{\vec\tau}_{\vec A}=\frac{A(v,a)}{B(v)},
\]
where $A(v,a)\in\mathbb Z[v,a^{\pm1}]$ and $B(v)$ is a product of the monic polynomials $\{m\}^2=vU_m(v)$.  Divide $vA(v,a)$ by $B(v)$ over $\mathbb Z[a^{\pm1}][v]$.  Rational polynomiality forces the remainder to vanish, so
\[
 vP^{\vec\tau}_{\vec A}\in\mathbb Z[v,a^{\pm1}].
\]
This proves Theorem~\ref{thm:framed-LMOV}.  Setting $\vec\tau=0$ recovers the zero-framed LMOV theorem.

label: lem:full-grid
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Write the second block exchange as $n$ rows.  Before row $r$ the active window contains unused high labels or low labels selected by previous rows.  The moving low label $r$ encounters descents exactly at unused high slots.  At a descent the Hecke rule permits either a swap or a stationary term with coefficient $z$.  Once stationarity is chosen at a high slot, the moving label becomes that high label; all remaining comparisons in the row are ascents, so no second stationary choice is possible.  Thus a path is exactly a partial injection and has coefficient $z^{|S|}$.  Distinct injections give distinct endpoint permutations.

For a full matching determined by $w\in S_n$, the endpoint is $(w^{-1}\oplus w)d$, where $d$ is the block exchange.  Its length is $n^2+2\ell(w)$, so the standard basis factorization is length-additive and summing over $w$ gives \eqref{eq:top-grid}.  The double-coset decomposition by the number of exchanged positions shows that each $R_k$ commutes with $A$.

title: Proof
body_md:
Choose matched subsets $S=\{s_0<\cdots<s_{k-1}\}$ and $T=\{t_0<\cdots<t_{k-1}\}$.  If $x=x_L\oplus x_R$ is the corresponding pair of minimal shuffles and $w\in S_k$ is the internal matching permutation, then a direct inversion count gives
\[
 \ell(xp_wx^{-1})=2\ell(x)+k^2+2\ell(w).
\]
Hence every displayed product is its positive standard basis element, and all size-$k$ partial matchings occur once.  The stationary $\mathsf{H}_m$ factors are disjoint from $\Delta_k$.  On a matched factor the Casimir sliding identity $a_L\Omega_k=\Omega_ka_R$ and block transport $a_RT_{d_k}=T_{d_k}a_L$ give $a_L\Delta_k=\Delta_ka_L$; similarly on the other side.

label: lem:higman
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:higman}
Let \(B\) be a split separable symmetric \(R_\alpha\)-algebra with unit Schur elements. Then the induced Higman map
\[
\bar h_B:M/[B,M]\rightarrow M^B
\]
is an isomorphism.
(See \cite[Sections~2.3--2.5]{LorenzTokoly}.)
If \(M\) is \(R_\alpha\)-free and
\(
h_B(y)\in\{n\}^aM,
\)
then
\[
y\in[B,M]+\{n\}^aM.
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The first statement is the Higman trace theorem. For the second statement, write
\[
h_B(y)=\{n\}^aY.
\]

Since \(h_B(y)\in M^B\) and \(M\) is \(R_\alpha\)-free, the relation
\[
\{n\}^a(bY-Yb)=0
\]
implies \(bY=Yb\) for all \(b\in B\). Hence \(Y\in M^B\). 

Because the induced Higman map
\(
\bar h_B:M/[B,M]\xrightarrow{\sim}M^B
\)
is an isomorphism, there exists
\(
x\in M
\)
such that
\(
h_B(x)=Y.
\)
Therefore:
\(
h_B(y-\{n\}^ax)=0.
\)
Hence:
\(
y-\{n\}^ax\in\ker h_B=[B,M].
\)
Therefore:
\(
y\in[B,M]+\{n\}^aM.
\)

label: lem:higman-square
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:higman-square}
The actual element $h_{\mathsf{H}}(b_n)$ belongs to $\{n\}^2\mathsf{H}$.
head: environment

label: eq:central-higman
title: Proof
body_md:
On a generic simple block, the Higman map is
$s_\lambda\operatorname{Tr}_\lambda$. The
Murnaghan--Nakayama rule \cite[Chapter~I, Section~7]{Macdonald}
says that the $n$-cycle character vanishes off hooks and is
$(-1)^j$ on $\eta_j$. Since $b_n$ closes to $\{n\}P_n$,
\[
 \operatorname{Tr}_{\eta_j}(b_n)=\{n\}(-1)^j,
 \qquad
 \operatorname{Tr}_\lambda(b_n)=0\quad
 (\lambda\text{ not a hook}).
\]
Writing $p_j$ for the generic central hook projectors gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:central-higman}
 z^n h_{\mathsf{H}}(b_n)
 =\{n\}^2\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}(-1)^jc_jp_j.
\end{equation}

An individual $p_j$ may have a simple pole. The projector
formula
\[
 p_\lambda=s_\lambda^{-1}
       \sum_{w\in S_n}\operatorname{Tr}_\lambda(T_w)T_{w^{-1}}
\]
has integral character coefficients. A hook of size $n$
has exactly one hook length $n$; a nonhook has none.
Thus $\{n\}p_j$ is regular, and the nonhook projectors
are regular. The total hook projector is regular as well.

Let $\omega=\alpha^n\in\{1,-1\}$. Successive ratios give
$c_{j+1}(\alpha)/c_j(\alpha)=-1$. The primitive product
identity gives
\[
 c_0(\alpha)
 =\alpha^{n(n-1)}\prod_{r=1}^{n-1}(1-\alpha^{-2r})
 =\varepsilon_n n.
\]
Here $\alpha^n=-1$ if $n$ is even, while $n-1$ is even if
$n$ is odd. Hence
\begin{equation}\label{eq:hook-coefficient-values}
 c_j(\alpha)=\varepsilon_n n(-1)^j.
\end{equation}
We may therefore write
\[
 \sum_j(-1)^jc_jp_j
 =\varepsilon_n n\sum_jp_j
  +\sum_j\bigl((-1)^jc_j-\varepsilon_n n\bigr)p_j.
\]
The first term is regular. Each coefficient in the second
sum is divisible by $\{n\}$, so each summand is a regular
multiple of $\{n\}p_j$. The bracket in
\eqref{eq:central-higman} is regular, and $z$ is a unit.
This proves the square factor.
head: environment

label: lem:transported-higman-square
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The map $\theta$ is an involutive $R_\alpha$-algebra
automorphism. Thus $t_{\mathsf{H}}^-$ is a perfect symmetric trace,
and $h_{\mathsf{H}}^-$ is an $R_\alpha$-linear map $\mathsf{H}\to \mathsf{H}$.
Twisting a generic simple Hecke module by $\theta$ transposes
its partition label. The Schur element for $t_{\mathsf{H}}^-$ on the
$\lambda$-block is consequently
\[
 s_\lambda^-=s_{\lambda^t}
 =q^{-\kappa_\lambda/2}
       \prod_{\square\in\lambda}\frac{\{h(\square)\}}z.
\]
The same $n$-cycle traces used above give
\eqref{eq:transported-higman-hooks}.

To descend this expression to the local lattice, note that
$c_j^-=q^{-\kappa_j}c_j$ and
$\alpha^{-\kappa_j}=\varepsilon_n$. Indeed,
$\kappa_j=n(n-1-2j)$; the second factor is even for odd
$n$, and is odd for even $n$, when $\alpha^n=-1$.
Together with \eqref{eq:hook-coefficient-values}, this gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:transported-hook-values}
 c_j^-(\alpha)=n(-1)^j,
 \qquad (-1)^jc_j^-(\alpha)=n.
\end{equation}
Let $p_{\mathrm{hook}}=\sum_jp_j$. As proved above,
$p_{\mathrm{hook}}$ and every $\{n\}p_j$ are regular.
The identity
\[
 \sum_j(-1)^jc_j^-p_j
 =np_{\mathrm{hook}}
  +\sum_j\bigl((-1)^jc_j^- -n\bigr)p_j
\]
therefore has a regular right side: every coefficient in
the second sum belongs to $\{n\}R_\alpha$. Since $z$ is
a unit, this proves \eqref{eq:transported-higman-square}.

For the norm statement, the transported coset systems are
dual because
\[
 t_{\mathsf{H}}^-\bigl(\theta(T_x)\theta(T_{y^{-1}})\bigr)
 =t_{\mathsf{H}}(T_xT_{y^{-1}}).
\]
Transporting the parabolic transitivity calculation proves
\eqref{eq:transported-transitivity}. The simple factors of a
proper Young subalgebra have size less than $n$, and their
transported Schur elements are units. Lemma~\ref{lem:higman},
applied with the transported trace, now gives
\eqref{eq:transported-norm-div}.

label: lem:full-swap
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:full-swap}
Let $\overline{\mathsf{H}}=\mathsf{H}/[\mathsf{H},\mathsf{H}]$, let $M_{\mathrm{sw}}=ACA$ be the full-swap double-coset bimodule, and let
\[
 \varsigma:\mathsf{H}\otimes \mathsf{H}\longrightarrow \mathsf{H}\otimes \mathsf{H},
 \qquad \varsigma(x\otimes y)=y\otimes x.
\]
Then multiplication by $C$ identifies $M_{\mathrm{sw}}$ with the twisted $A$-bimodule ${}_1A_\varsigma$, and the map
\begin{equation}\label{eq:full-swap-map}
 \Phi_{\mathrm{sw}}:
 M_{\mathrm{sw}}/[A,M_{\mathrm{sw}}]\longrightarrow\overline{\mathsf{H}},
 \qquad [x_Ly_RC]\longmapsto[xy]
\end{equation}
is an $R_\alpha$-module isomorphism.  Under this isomorphism the full-matching component of
\[
 b_Lb_R(C^2-1)-\varepsilon_n n\{n\}^2b_LC
\]
is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:full-swap-explicit}
 \{n\}^2\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}
 \bigl(c_j-\varepsilon_n n(-1)^j\bigr)f_j.
\end{equation}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The relations $Ca=\varsigma(a)C$ for $a\in A$ give $ACA=AC$ and identify $u\in A$ with $uC\in M_{\mathrm{sw}}$.  Under this identification,
\[
 [A,M_{\mathrm{sw}}]
 \longleftrightarrow
 \left\langle au-u\varsigma(a):a,u\in A\right\rangle_{R_\alpha}.
\]
Thus the relative cocenter is the twisted coinvariant module
\[
 A_\varsigma:=A/\left\langle au-u\varsigma(a)\right\rangle_{R_\alpha}.
\]
Let $m:A=\mathsf{H}\otimes \mathsf{H}\to\overline{\mathsf{H}}$ be $m(x\otimes y)=[xy]$.  For
$a=a_1\otimes a_2$ and $u=u_1\otimes u_2$,
\[
 m(au-u\varsigma(a))
 =[a_1u_1a_2u_2-u_1a_2u_2a_1]=0,
\]
so $m$ descends to $\Phi_{\mathrm{sw}}$.  It is surjective.  Define
\[
 s:\overline{\mathsf{H}}\longrightarrow A_\varsigma,
 \qquad [h]\longmapsto[h\otimes1].
\]
In $A_\varsigma$ the defining relations give
\[
 [x\otimes y]=[xy\otimes1]=[1\otimes yx]=[yx\otimes1].
\]
Hence $s$ kills commutators and is well defined.  The same identities show
$\Phi_{\mathrm{sw}}\circ s=\mathrm{id}_{\overline{\mathsf{H}}}$ and
$s\circ\Phi_{\mathrm{sw}}=\mathrm{id}_{A_\varsigma}$.  Therefore \eqref{eq:full-swap-map} is bijective.

By Lemma~\ref{lem:full-grid}, the full-matching part of $C^2-1$ is $z^nR_n=z^n\Omega_{\mathsf{H}}C$.  Hence, using $R_n=\Omega_{\mathsf{H}}C$ and the definition of the Higman map,
\begin{align*}
 \Phi_{\mathrm{sw}}\bigl(z^n b_Lb_RR_n\bigr)
 &=z^n\left[\sum_{w\in S_n}bT_wbT_{w^{-1}}\right]\\
 &=z^n[b\,h_{\mathsf{H}}(b)].
\end{align*}
In the generic cocenter, \eqref{eq:central-higman}  gives
\[
 z^n h_{\mathsf{H}}(b)=\{n\}^2\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}(-1)^jc_jp_j.
\]
The annular closure of $b$ is
\[
 B_n=\{n\}P_n=\{n\}\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}(-1)^jQ_j,
\]
so the $\eta_j$-block of the cocenter class of $b$ is
\[
 [p_jb]=(-1)^j\{n\}Q_j=(-1)^jf_j.
\]
Consequently
\begin{equation}\label{eq:full-first-contribution}
 \Phi_{\mathrm{sw}}\bigl(z^n b_Lb_RR_n\bigr)
 =\{n\}^2\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}c_jf_j.
\end{equation}
Similarly,
\[
 \Phi_{\mathrm{sw}}(b_LC)=[b]
 =\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}(-1)^jf_j.
\]
Subtracting $\varepsilon_n n\{n\}^2\Phi_{\mathrm{sw}}(b_LC)$ from \eqref{eq:full-first-contribution} proves \eqref{eq:full-swap-explicit}.  The calculation was written using generic central projectors only to separate simple blocks.  Both sides of \eqref{eq:full-swap-explicit} are regular, and the integral type-$A$ cocenter is free over the local ring; hence the equality descends to the regular cocenter lattice.

title: Proof
body_md:
Use \eqref{eq:full-grid}.  For $0<k<n$, the $k$th double-coset component of $b_Lb_R(C^2-1)$ is $z^kb_Lb_RR_k$.  By the shuffle formula and cyclic sliding in $\mathsf{G}/[A,\mathsf{G}]$,
\[
 [b_Lb_RR_k]
 =\bigl[N_{B_L}^\mathsf{H}(b)_L\,N_{B_R}^\mathsf{H}(b)_R\,\Delta_k\bigr].
\]
Transitivity and Lemmas \ref{lem:higman}, \ref{lem:higman-square} imply
\[
 N_{B_L}^\mathsf{H}(b)\equiv\{n\}^2y_L\pmod{[B_L,\mathsf{H}]},\qquad
 N_{B_R}^\mathsf{H}(b)\equiv\{n\}^2y_R\pmod{[B_R,\mathsf{H}]}.
\]
Because $\Delta_k$ commutes with $B_k$, each replacement is legal in the relative quotient.  Hence every proper component is divisible by $\{n\}^4$.

The bottom component is zero.  By Lemma~\ref{lem:full-swap}, the full-swap component is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:mixed-top}
 \{n\}^2\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}a_jf_j,
 \qquad
 a_j=c_j-\varepsilon_n n(-1)^j.
\end{equation}
Each $a_j$ vanishes at $\alpha$, hence $a_j\in\{n\}R_\alpha$.  Moreover
\[
 \sum_j(-1)^ja_j\in\{n\}^2R_\alpha.
\]
Indeed its value is zero by $c_j(\alpha)=\varepsilon_n n(-1)^j$, and its first $q$-derivative is zero because
\[
 \sum_j\frac{q c_j'}{c_j}
 =\frac12\sum_j\kappa_j+2\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}(n-j)L_j=0
\]
by \eqref{eq:derivative-cancel}.  Substituting \eqref{eq:hook-lattice} gives the explicit decomposition
\[
 \{n\}^2\sum_ja_jf_j
 =\{n\}^2\left(\sum_j(-1)^ja_j\right)f_0
 +\{n\}^3\sum_ja_jr_j,
\]
and both terms lie in $\{n\}^4\overline{\mathsf{H}}$.  Since $\Phi_{\mathrm{sw}}$ is an $R_\alpha$-module isomorphism, its inverse carries $\{n\}^4\overline{\mathsf{H}}$ onto $\{n\}^4(M_{\mathrm{sw}}/[A,M_{\mathrm{sw}}])$.  Hence the original full-swap class lies in
\[
 [A,M_{\mathrm{sw}}]+\{n\}^4M_{\mathrm{sw}}
 \subset [A,\mathsf{G}]+\{n\}^4\mathsf{G}.
\]
This is precisely the divisibility needed for the top component.

label: lem:self-full
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:self-full}
After applying $\theta$ to the full-grid identity, the
full-matching contribution to the self remainder, viewed
in $\overline{\mathsf{H}}\otimes\overline{\mathsf{H}}$, is, apart from the
factor $\varepsilon_n$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:self-full-tensor}
 \sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\delta_jf_j\otimes f_j
 -\left(\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}(-1)^jf_j\right)^{\otimes2},
 \qquad
 \delta_j=(-1)^jc_j^-.
\end{equation}

label: eq:inverse-grid
title: Proof
body_md:
Since $\theta(C)=(-1)^nC^{-1}$, applying $\theta$ to
\eqref{eq:full-grid} gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:inverse-grid}
 C-C^{-1}=-\sum_{k=1}^nz^kC\theta(R_k).
\end{equation}
As $R_n=\Omega_{\mathsf{H}}C$, the $k=n$ term returns to the identity
double-coset summand $A$. The quotient of that summand is
\[
 A/[A,A]\cong\overline{\mathsf{H}}\otimes_{R_\alpha}\overline{\mathsf{H}}.
\]
Indeed,
$[A,A]=[\mathsf{H},\mathsf{H}]\otimes \mathsf{H}+\mathsf{H}\otimes[\mathsf{H},\mathsf{H}]$, as follows by
expanding commutators of pure tensors and by setting one
factor equal to $1$ for the converse inclusion.

Conjugating the transported Casimir through the block
exchange gives, up to $\varepsilon_n$,
\[
 z^n\sum_{w\in S_n}b\theta(T_{w^{-1}})\otimes\theta(T_w).
\]
We evaluate this tensor over the generic split semisimple
field. On the block of shape $\lambda$, the transported
trace has Schur element $s_\lambda^-$, and its Casimir is
\[
 s_\lambda^-\sum_{u,v}E_{uv}\otimes E_{vu}.
\]
With $b$ inserted in the first factor, projection to the
tensor cocenter gives
\[
 s_\lambda^-\operatorname{Tr}_\lambda(b)
                      Q_\lambda\otimes Q_\lambda.
\]
There is no dimension factor, since $Q_\lambda$ is the
class of a primitive idempotent. The second trace forces
$u=v$, and the first then sums the diagonal entries of $b$.

The $n$-cycle trace vanishes off hooks. On $\eta_j$,
\[
 \operatorname{Tr}_{\eta_j}(b)=\{n\}(-1)^j,
 \qquad
 s_{\eta_j}^-=q^{-\kappa_j/2}
       \frac{\{n\}\{n-j-1\}!\{j\}!}{z^n}.
\]
Multiplication by $z^n$ and $f_j=\{n\}Q_j$ give precisely
$\delta_jf_j\otimes f_j$. The unmixed product has class
\[
 [b]\otimes[b]
 =\left(\sum_j(-1)^jf_j\right)^{\otimes2}.
\]
This proves \eqref{eq:self-full-tensor} generically. Its two
sides are regular, and the ordinary cocenter and its
tensor square are free over $R_\alpha$. The equality
therefore descends to the local tensor lattice.

label: eq:self-relative-duality
title: Proof
body_md:
We first prove the assertion about $S_k$. Put
\[
 W_k=C\theta(\Delta_k),\qquad
 \Xi_k=\sum_{x_L\in\mathcal D_L}E_{x_L,k}.
\]
For $B=B_L$, let $\mathsf E_B:\mathsf{H}\to B$ be the canonical
parabolic projection in the standard basis. Its transported
version is
$\mathsf E_B^-=\theta|_B\circ\mathsf E_B\circ\theta$.
The distinguished right coset systems
\[
 u_x=\theta(T_x),\qquad v_x=\theta(T_{x^{-1}}),
 \qquad x\in\mathcal D_L,
\]
are relative Frobenius dual bases. Explicitly, standard-basis
duality and the decomposition $w=xu$ give, for $h\in \mathsf{H}$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:self-relative-duality}
 h=\sum_xu_x\mathsf E_B^-(v_xh)
  =\sum_x\mathsf E_B^-(hu_x)v_x.
\end{equation}
The relative Casimir
\[
 \mathcal E_B^-=\sum_xu_x\otimes_Bv_x
                   \in \mathsf{H}\otimes_B\mathsf{H}
\]
therefore satisfies $h\mathcal E_B^-=\mathcal E_B^-h$
for every $h\in \mathsf{H}$. To see this directly, use the two
expansions in \eqref{eq:self-relative-duality}:
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 h\mathcal E_B^-
 &=\sum_{x,y}u_y\mathsf E_B^-(v_yhu_x)\otimes_Bv_x\\
 &=\sum_yu_y\otimes_B
                \left(\sum_x\mathsf E_B^-(v_yhu_x)v_x\right)\\
 &=\sum_yu_y\otimes_Bv_yh=\mathcal E_B^-h.
 \end{aligned}
\]

For $c\in B_L$, block transport and commutation with
$\theta(\Delta_k)$ give $c_RW_k=W_kc_L$.
The map
\[
 \mathsf{H}\otimes_{B_L}\mathsf{H}\longrightarrow M_k,
 \qquad u\otimes v\longmapsto u_RW_kv_L
\]
is consequently balanced, and sends $\mathcal E_{B_L}^-$
to $\Xi_k$. The Casimir identity proves
\begin{equation}\label{eq:self-full-packet-intertwining}
 h_R\Xi_k=\Xi_kh_L\qquad(h\in \mathsf{H}).
\end{equation}
On the other hand, \eqref{eq:self-pointwise-intertwining} gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:self-proper-packet-intertwining}
 c_L\Xi_k=\Xi_kc_R\qquad(c\in B_R).
\end{equation}
For $c\in B_R$ and $h\in \mathsf{H}$, cyclicity in $M_k/[A,M_k]$
and these two identities imply
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 [(c_Lh_L-h_Lc_L)\Xi_k]
 &=[h_L\Xi_kc_L-h_L\Xi_kc_R]\\
 &=[h_Lc_R\Xi_k-h_L\Xi_kc_R]\\
 &=[c_Rh_L\Xi_k-h_L\Xi_kc_R]=0.
 \end{aligned}
\]
The last expression is an $A$-commutator. Thus the map
factors through $\mathsf{H}/[B_R,\mathsf{H}]$, proving
\eqref{eq:self-transfer-map}. Interchanging the packets proves
the right-handed statement.

We prove the divisibility assertions on the full
$A$-bimodule $\mathsf{G}$. For any symmetric trace on $\mathsf{H}$, let
$e_i,e_i^*$ be dual bases and put
$\Omega=\sum_i e_i\otimes e_i^*$. Casimir duality gives
$\Omega(1\otimes x)=(x\otimes1)\Omega$. Consequently
\begin{equation}\label{eq:self-tensor-higman}
 \begin{aligned}
 \sum_{i,j}e_i^*be_j\otimes e_j^*e_i
 &=\sum_i(e_i^*b\otimes1)\Omega(1\otimes e_i)\\
 &=\sum_i(e_i^*be_i\otimes1)\Omega\\
 &=(h_{\mathsf{H}}(b)\otimes1)\Omega.
 \end{aligned}
\end{equation}
This is an identity in the actual tensor algebra.

Apply it to the transported trace $t_{\mathsf{H}}^-$ and write
$\Omega_{\mathsf{H}}^-=\theta(\Omega_{\mathsf{H}})$. The tensor-product trace
on $A$ has transported dual bases
$(e_i)_L(e_j)_R$ and $(e_i^*)_L(e_j^*)_R$. Block transport
therefore gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:self-full-higman}
 \begin{aligned}
 h_A^-(b_LC)
 &=\sum_{i,j}(e_i^*)_L(e_j^*)_R\,b_LC(e_i)_L(e_j)_R\\
 &=\sum_{i,j}(e_i^*be_j)_L(e_j^*e_i)_R\,C\\
 &=(h_{\mathsf{H}}^-(b)\otimes1)\Omega_{\mathsf{H}}^-C.
 \end{aligned}
\end{equation}
Lemma~\ref{lem:transported-higman-square} proves that this belongs to
$\{n\}^2\mathsf{G}$.

The traces on $B_k\subset A$ are compatible. Transporting
the right coset decomposition $w=xu$ gives
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 h_{B_k}^-N_{B_k}^{A,-}(y)
 &=\sum_{u\in W(B_k)}\sum_{x\in\mathcal D_k}
   \theta(T_{u^{-1}})\theta(T_{x^{-1}})
             y\theta(T_x)\theta(T_u)\\
 &=\sum_{w\in W(A)}\theta(T_{w^{-1}})y\theta(T_w)
  =h_A^-(y).
 \end{aligned}
\]
Every factor of $B_k$ has size $k$ or $n-k$, strictly
less than $n$. Its transported Schur elements are therefore
units. The module $\mathsf{G}$ is free over $R_\alpha$. Applying
Lemma~\ref{lem:higman} to \eqref{eq:self-full-higman}
proves \eqref{eq:self-norm-square}.

Finally, apply $\theta$ to the shuffle formula and move
the trailing shuffle around the relative cocenter:
\begin{equation}\label{eq:self-pairing}
 \begin{aligned}
 [b_LC\theta(R_k)]
 &=\sum_{x\in\mathcal D_k}
   [b_LC\theta(T_x)\theta(\Delta_k)\theta(T_{x^{-1}})]\\
 &=\sum_{x\in\mathcal D_k}
   [\theta(T_{x^{-1}})b_LC\theta(T_x)\theta(\Delta_k)]\\
 &=[N_{B_k}^{A,-}(b_LC)\theta(\Delta_k)].
 \end{aligned}
\end{equation}
The cyclic step is valid because $\theta(T_{x^{-1}})\in A$.
Since $\theta$ preserves $B_k$, the element
$\theta(\Delta_k)$ commutes with $B_k$. Thus, for
$x\in B_k$ and $Y\in \mathsf{G}$,
\[
 [x,Y]\theta(\Delta_k)=[x,Y\theta(\Delta_k)]\in[A,\mathsf{G}].
\]
Substituting \eqref{eq:self-norm-square} into
\eqref{eq:self-pairing} proves
\eqref{eq:self-proper-divisibility}.

The map $S_k$ also records the one-packet norm transfer.
Expand the shuffle formula with
$x=x_L\oplus x_R$:
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 [b_LC\theta(R_k)]
 =\sum_{x_L\in\mathcal D_L}\sum_{x_R\in\mathcal D_R}
 \bigl[&b_LC\theta(T_{x_L,L})\theta(T_{x_R,R})\theta(\Delta_k)\\
      &\hspace{1em}\cdot\theta(T_{x_L^{-1},L})
                         \theta(T_{x_R^{-1},R})\bigr].
 \end{aligned}
\]
For each $x_R\in\mathcal D_R$, write
$u=\theta(T_{x_R})$ and $v=\theta(T_{x_R^{-1}})$.
After summing over $x_L$, its contribution is
$[b_Lu_L\Xi_kv_R]$. In the relative quotient,
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 [b_Lu_L\Xi_kv_R]
 &=[v_Rb_Lu_L\Xi_k]
  =[b_Lu_Lv_R\Xi_k]\\
 &=[b_Lu_L\Xi_kv_L]
  =[v_Lb_Lu_L\Xi_k],
 \end{aligned}
\]
where the middle step uses
\eqref{eq:self-full-packet-intertwining} for $v\in \mathsf{H}$.
Summing over $x_R$ gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:self-packet-norm}
 [b_LC\theta(R_k)]
 =\sum_{x_L\in\mathcal D_L}
       \bigl[(N_{B_R}^{\mathsf{H},-}(b))_LE_{x_L,k}\bigr]
\end{equation}
and hence
\begin{equation}\label{eq:self-packet-transfer}
 [b_LC\theta(R_k)]
 =S_k\bigl([N_{B_R}^{\mathsf{H},-}(b)]\bigr)
       \quad\text{in }M_k/[A,M_k].
\end{equation}
By \eqref{eq:transported-norm-div},
$[N_{B_R}^{\mathsf{H},-}(b)]=\{n\}^2[y_R]$ in $\mathsf{H}/[B_R,\mathsf{H}]$.
Thus the same proper component is $\{n\}^2S_k([y_R])$.

label: eq:self-remaining
title: Proof
body_md:
By \eqref{eq:inverse-grid} and Lemma~\ref{lem:self-proper},
every proper component of $b_L(C-C^{-1})$ belongs to
$[A,\mathsf{G}]+\{n\}^2\mathsf{G}$. The remaining full-matching term returns
to $A$: indeed,
\[
 C\theta(R_n)=(-1)^n\Omega_{\mathsf{H}}^-,
\]
because packet exchange preserves the symmetric tensor
$\Omega_{\mathsf{H}}^-$. Hence the remaining self remainder is
represented by
\[
 \varepsilon_n\bigl(z^nb_L\Omega_{\mathsf{H}}^- -b_Lb_R\bigr).
\]
By Lemma~\ref{lem:self-full}, its class, apart from
$\varepsilon_n$, is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:self-remaining}
 \sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\delta_jf_j\otimes f_j
 -\left(\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}(-1)^jf_j\right)^{\otimes2}.
\end{equation}

At the root, $\delta_j(\alpha)=n$ for every $j$.
One may see this either from \eqref{eq:transported-hook-values}
or from
\[
 \frac{\delta_{j+1}}{\delta_j}
 =-q^n\frac{\{j+1\}}{\{n-j-1\}},\qquad
 \delta_0(\alpha)
 =\prod_{r=1}^{n-1}(1-\alpha^{-2r})=n.
\]
Furthermore,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:self-delta-sum}
 \sum_j\delta_j-n^2\in\{n\}^2R_\alpha.
\end{equation}
The value at $\alpha$ is zero. The logarithmic derivatives
satisfy
\[
 \sum_j\frac{q\delta_j'}{\delta_j}
 =-\frac12\sum_j\kappa_j
   +2\sum_{r=1}^{n-1}(n-r)L_r,
\]
which vanishes at $\alpha$ by \eqref{eq:derivative-cancel}.
Since every $\delta_j(\alpha)=n$, the ordinary derivative
of $\sum_j\delta_j-n^2$ also vanishes, proving
\eqref{eq:self-delta-sum}.

Insert $f_j=(-1)^jf_0+\{n\}r_j$ into
\eqref{eq:self-remaining} and put
$r_* =\sum_j(-1)^jr_j$. The result is
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 &\left(\sum_j\delta_j-n^2\right)f_0\otimes f_0\\
 &\quad+\{n\}\sum_j(-1)^j(\delta_j-n)
                      (f_0\otimes r_j+r_j\otimes f_0)\\
 &\quad+\{n\}^2
       \left(\sum_j\delta_jr_j\otimes r_j-r_*\otimes r_*\right).
 \end{aligned}
\]
The first coefficient belongs to $\{n\}^2R_\alpha$,
and $\delta_j-n\in\{n\}R_\alpha$. Every term is therefore
divisible by $\{n\}^2$ in
$\overline{\mathsf{H}}\otimes\overline{\mathsf{H}}$, and hence in its image
in $\mathsf{G}/[A,\mathsf{G}]$. This proves the self identity.

\label{rem:small-checks}
For $n=2$, the hooks are $(2)$ and $(1,1)$, with
\[
 \kappa_0=2,\qquad \kappa_1=-2,\qquad
 c_0=q\{1\},\qquad c_1=q^{-1}\{1\}.
\]
At an exact squared-order-two root,
\[
 c_j(\alpha)=-2(-1)^j=\varepsilon_2\,2(-1)^j,
 \qquad
 \left.q\frac{d}{dq}(c_0-c_1)\right|_{q=\alpha}=0.
\]
The self coefficients satisfy
$\delta_0(\alpha)=\delta_1(\alpha)=2$.

For $n=3$, the three hooks have
\[
 (\kappa_0,\kappa_1,\kappa_2)=(6,0,-6),
\]
and
\[
 (c_0,c_1,c_2)
 =\bigl(q^3\{2\}\{1\},\ \{1\}^2,\ q^{-3}\{2\}\{1\}\bigr).
\]
At an exact squared-order-three root,
$c_j(\alpha)=3(-1)^j$ and $\delta_j(\alpha)=3$.
Direct substitution gives
\[
 \sum_j(-1)^ja_j\in\{3\}^2R_\alpha,
 \qquad
 \sum_j\delta_j-9\in\{3\}^2R_\alpha.
\]
These computations check the normalization and signs in
both full-matching formulas.

title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:composite}
No primality assumption occurs in Theorem~\ref{thm:relative-hecke}.
The cyclotomic inputs are $\{j\}(\alpha)\ne0$ for
$0<j<n$ when $\operatorname{ord}(\alpha^2)=n$, and the primitive product
identity for $\alpha^2$. The local theorem therefore applies
to composite packet sizes as well. For composite $n$, the
passage from local divisibility by $\{n\}^2$ at an exact
squared-order-$n$ root to a global congruence modulo $U_n(v)$
also requires the roots of proper-divisor squared order.
Those roots are treated separately in the global argument.
